name: Moro
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Jenks, Peter, Elyasir Julima, Angelo Naser & Sharon Rose. Forthcoming (proofreading version dated 2025-11-27). A grammar of Moro (with a focus on the Thetogovela dialect). catalog_locator: Grammar sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress', pp. 47-48; tone system Ch. 4, p. 95. NLLT 2011: pp. 228, 234, 246.
catalog_quote: Black & Black (1971: 14) mention a correlation between vowel lengthening and stress in Moro: Stress presents a problem because it fluctuates freely in many words. It also seems to vary with the intonation pattern and is affected by elision. However for the most part a rough prediction can be given. 1. If the last syllable is closed, it is stressed. 2. If it is open the stress moves to the pentultimate unless this syllable contains /ə/. 3. If so the stress moves further to the front to the nearest syllable not containing /ə/, or, 4. If the word is only 2 syllable, the stress returns to the ultimate. ... It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress, since high pitch is an acoustic correlate of stress in English. ... If Moro has stress, tone is not a correlate of stress. Any type of syllable (open/closed) and any type of vowel may bear either high or low tone. ... based on the results here, duration does not appear to be tied to position in a systematic way. If pitch and duration do not convey stress, other factors such as intensity, consonant production or vowel quality might be indicators of prominence. We have not conducted an instrumental study to determine this, and at this point, the question of whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind is left undetermined.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Moro (moro1285) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Jenks & Rose 2011 NLLT 'High tone in Moro', was obtained in full as an open-access PDF (via the rd.springer.com mirror; saved and logged). It is a tone paper: Moro has privative H vs. L; stress appears only comparatively (pp. 228-229: duration/intensity evidence for feet 'not strong'; p. 234: H follows a (C)VC > CV > V prominence scale 'similar to stress systems'; p. 246: verb H is 'stress-like', noun H 'tone-like'). It makes no claim about word-stress placement. The best first-hand stress statement remains the Jenks, Julima, Naser & Rose LangSci grammar sec. 2.1.14 (already held by the project, re-read): it quotes Black & Black's 1971 stress rules (closed ultima, else penult, /ə/-avoidance), argues they are likely misheard tone, reports no systematic duration-by-position effect, and leaves 'whether Moro has stress or prominence of some kind.. undetermined'. Black & Black 1971 (print only, Khartoum) is the only source asserting stress and is low priority since its stress passage is quoted in full in the grammar. Nothing here contradicts anything, since there is no catalog record; recommended coding: tone language, word stress undetermined.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the copy consulted (788 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A grammar of Moro', authors Jenks/Julima/Naser/Rose, created 2025-11-27; CC BY 4.0 LangSci proofreading version served openly from github.com/langsci/569 gh-pages). Sec. 2.1.14 'Vowel Length and Stress' is on printed pp. 47-48 (pp. 71-72) exactly as located. Every sentence of the reported quote is present verbatim: 'It is not clear what Black & Black (1971) perceive to be stress in Moro. They did not recognize Moro to be a tone language in their grammar, and as English speakers, they may have interpreted pitch differences as stress, since high pitch is an acoustic correlate of stress in English.'.. 'If Moro has stress,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Moro is a two-tone (H vs L, privative H) language. The modern reference grammar finds no evidence for word stress: tone is independent of syllable type/position, a pilot duration study shows no systematic penult/final lengthening, and the existence of stress or any non-tonal prominence is explicitly left undetermined. The only positive stress rule in the literature is Black & Black 1971:14 (final syllable if closed, else penult unless it contains /ə/, then the nearest non-ə syllable further left; disyllables revert to final), which the grammar quotes and attributes to misheard H tone plus phrase-final lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Black & Black 1971 (as quoted): stress 'fluctuates freely in many words', varies with intonation and elision; vowel lengthening under stress only in isolation forms. Grammar: one of four disyllabic nouns (ðáɾá) showed a significantly longer final vowel; trisyllable durations depend on the intervening consonant, not position; phrase-final lengthening exists only in story/list intonation (sec. 4.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress is the topic; the grammar suggests B&B's lengthening reflects isolation/utterance-final (phrase-level) position rather than word-internal stress. Duration measurements were on nouns in phrase-final position of SVO carrier sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Thetogovela variety of Moro (language-level glottocode moro1285; dialect-level glottocode not verified). Black & Black 1971, whose stress rules the grammar quotes and disputes, described a different (Umm Dorein-area) variety per the grammar's framing; both are Moro [mor].

tone_statements.citation: Chung, Younah, Page Piccinini & Sharon Rose. 2016. The interaction of polar question and declarative intonation with lexical tone in Moro. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2016 (Boston), 615-619. ISCA.
tone_statements.quote: Moro has two contrastive tones, high (H) and low (L), as shown by the following minimal pairs. Low tone is unmarked. All data are from the Thetogovela dialect of Moro. (1) Nal@Na ‘song’ waRá ‘baobab tree’ Nál´@Ná ‘kingdom’ wáRá ‘chicken’ … there is a significant drop in the H tone of the verb in the declarative utterances compared to questions. This suggests that an automatic downstep of the second H is suspended in questions, as in Hausa [7]
tone_statements.locator: p. 615, sec. 1 Introduction (inventory + minimal pairs); p. 617, sec. 4 Discussion (downstep)
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones, high and low (low unmarked), shown by minimal pairs; F0 study of two speakers: tone targets kept in questions; automatic downstep of a second H; final L boundary tone.

tone_statements.citation: Jenks, Peter & Sharon Rose. 2015. Mobile object markers in Moro: The role of tone. Language 91(2): 269-307. Linguistic Society of America.
tone_statements.quote: Moro has two basic surface tones, high (H) and low (L). Underlyingly, Moro is an H/∅ tone system; L tone is not active (Jenks & Rose 2011). In the verbal system, verb roots do not show H versus L lexical tone contrasts. Instead, there are three distinct patterns of grammatical tone on Moro verb stems. … If these prefixal H tones are adjacent to default H on the root, the H on the root may be downstepped (marked with ꜜ).
tone_statements.locator: p. 275, sec. 3 'Tone properties of verb stems and the position of OMs'; downstep sentence p. 279, sec. 3.3
tone_statements.summary: Two surface tones, high and low; underlyingly privative H vs zero (L inactive). Verb roots lack lexical tone: three grammatical stem patterns (default H, all-H, no-H); H downstepped at macrostem edge.

tone_statements.citation: Rose, Sharon. 2013. The morphological structure of the Moro verb. In Thilo C. Schadeberg & Roger M. Blench (eds.), Nuba Mountain Language Studies, 25-56. Cologne: Ruediger Koeppe.
tone_statements.quote: The proximal imperative is formed from the verb root and a final suffix -ó. All tone-bearing units in the proximal imperative verb stem bear high tone, which is marked with an acute accent (´). Low tone is unmarked. Moro has a two tone system, High (H) and Low (L). Jenks & Rose (2011) analyze it as a H vs. Ø system, where Ø is unmarked.
tone_statements.locator: manuscript p. 3, sec. 2.1 'Imperative'; downstep: p. 10 sec. 3 and p. 17 sec. 5.1 fn. 11
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low (H vs zero analysis); verbs take predictable default H or aspect/mood melodies (all-H, all-L, L-H, H-L-H); downstep between H tones at the macrostem edge.

tone_statements.citation: Strabone, Andrew & Sharon Rose. 2012. Morphophonological properties of Moro causatives. In Bruce Connell & Nicholas Rolle (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 41st Annual Conference on African Linguistics: African Languages in Contact, 92-103. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
tone_statements.quote: Moro verb stems fall into two distinct classes according to aspect/mood: those in which lexical high tone appears on the root and those that have specific melodic or inflectional tone patterns. In this section, we show that the causative imposes its own particular tone pattern, H-L, and how that tone pattern interacts with lexical tone and melodic tone. We assume a H/Ø tone contrast (Jenks & Rose 2011, to appear), although we use the label L to indicate lack of high tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 98, Sec. 5 'Tone' (opening paragraph); also p. 92 Sec. 1 'We mark high tone only throughout the paper'; downstep p. 101 ex. (28c); (and pp. 1, 10)
tone_statements.summary: Privative two-way contrast, high vs. no high (written L); lexical H on verb roots spreads by syllable weight; causative and aspect/mood affixes impose H-L, L-H, H-H, L-L melodies; downstep between Hs.

tone_statements.quote: in Moro (Kordofanian: Sudan), a left-aligned high tone is epenthesized on all verb stems (in brackets), but only in certain inflectional categories of the verb (Jenks and Rose 2011). In (1), this tone occurs on the leftmost syllable, underlined, of imperfective verbs stems (1a), but not in perfective verbs such as (1b). The all-L venitive imperative form in (1c) shows that the absence of this H tone cannot simply be attributed to the presence of a final H suffix.

tone_statements.summary: Imperfective verb stems carry an inserted stem-initial H that perfective and venitive-imperative stems lack, while the preverb (subject agreement, tense) keeps its own tone whatever the aspect. Data are secondary (Rose 2013; Jenks & Rose 2015) and modelled as a v-head cophonology; this adds the aspect-conditioned verb-stem melody to the catalog's H/L contrast entry.

sources.quote: It would be preferable if there were independent arguments for feet, such as intensity or vowel duration, but there is a lack of clear evidence. Short verb roots typically contain a vowel that is longer than surrounding vowels: [kawáðá] 'poke', a property that is often associated with primary stress. Yet long verb roots typically contain a schwa in one of the two positions making vowel duration comparisons difficult. [...] Thus, while the duration facts are suggestive of a trochaic foot aligned with the left edge of the root, the evidence is not strong.
sources.locator: pp. 228-229 (Sect. 4.1, foot-based analysis of tone doubling); also p. 234 (Sect. 4.2) and p. 246 (conclusion)
sources.note: A tone paper (privative H vs. L, Thetogovela dialect), not a stress paper. Stress enters only comparatively: on pp. 228-229 the authors look for phonetic correlates (duration, intensity) of the bimoraic foot they use to model binary H spreading in verbs, find a longer root-initial vowel in short verb roots ('a property that is often associated with primary stress') but call the evidence 'not strong' and intensity 'inconclusive'; on p. 234 they say H distribution in D-stems follows a syllable-prominence scale (C)VC > CV > V 'similar to stress systems that show both rime and onset sensitivity';…

sources.quote: Stress presents a problem because it fluctuates freely in many words. It also seems to vary with the intonation pattern and is affected by elision. However for the most part a rough prediction can be given. 1. If the last syllable is closed, it is stressed. 2. If it is open the stress moves to the pentultimate unless this syllable contains /ə/. 3. If so the stress moves further to the front to the nearest syllable not containing /ə/, or, 4. If the word is only 2 syllable, the stress returns to the ultimate. (as quoted in Jenks et al., sec. 2.1.14, p. 47)
